analysis.one_liner: Caps US prescription drug prices at 6% above the average price in five other wealthy countries.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by one House member with no cosponsors, sent to two committees, and never received a vote before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ordered the President to set rules ensuring no drug sold to US consumers costs more than 6% above the average retail price in the five most industrialized free-market countries besides the US. It would give federal officers subpoena power to examine drug company records, allow civil penalties up to 200% of unjust enrichment, criminal fines for knowing violations, and let consumers sue for damages and attorney's fees, including through class actions.
analysis.who_benefits: American consumers who pay retail prices for prescription drugs, which are often far higher than prices for the same drugs in countries like Canada, France, Germany, Japan, and the UK. Anyone overcharged would be able to recover damages and legal fees in court.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the price of any pharmaceutical product sold to US consumers at 6% above the average retail price in the five most industrialized free-market countries other than the US, as determined by the President.
Gives enforcement officers power to examine drug company books and records, issue subpoenas, and refer refusals to the Attorney General for court enforcement.
Allows civil penalties of up to 200% of unjust enrichment, with each overpriced sale counted as a separate violation, and criminal fines up to 200% of the sale amount for knowing violations.
Lets consumers who were overcharged sue for actual damages or the amount paid, plus court-allowed additional damages, attorneys' fees, and class action remedies.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose US revenues would fall toward the lower prices they already charge in other countries, and who would face new federal price enforcement, penalties, and private lawsuits.

drawbacks.text: The bill gives the President sweeping discretion to define which products are covered, which five countries set the benchmark, and what the average retail price is, all without detailed statutory standards.

Enforcement would rest on agencies the President chooses, with final penalty assessments that are unappealable if a hearing is not requested in 20 days, raising due-process and administrative-burden concerns.

Critics of international reference pricing argue that lower US prices could reduce revenue available for developing new drugs, a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge; this argument is a general policy debate, not drawn from the provided sources.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the potential benefit is large: drug prices in the US are among the highest in the world, and this bill would directly tie them to lower prices charged abroad, backed by penalties and private lawsuits. The costs fall on pharmaceutical companies, though supporters of the industry would argue reduced revenues could eventually affect drug development. The bill's design is crude — heavy delegation to the President and aggressive penalty provisions — but its core effect would shift billions in costs from consumers to drug makers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees, then to the Health Subcommittee, and sat there until the 109th Congress ended without any committee action or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Major Owens introduced the bill on March 2, 2006.
It was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and, in addition, to the Committee on the Judiciary for consideration of provisions within each committee's jurisdiction.
On March 17, 2006, it was referred to the Health Subcommittee, and no further action followed.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and the bill was never reported out of committee or voted on by either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers are better off: US drug prices were never capped by this bill, and no federal price enforcement or consumer litigation based on it followed. American consumers continue to pay the same prices they would have paid without it.

for.name: Rep. Major Owens
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill on March 2, 2006.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 2, 2006 and sent it to the Health Subcommittee; never reported the bill or scheduled consideration.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 2, 2006; never took further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: With a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no votes, the bill generated no visible partisan split in the record.

industries.note: The bill would cap US retail drug prices near the lower levels already charged in five other wealthy countries, backed by penalties of up to 200% of unjust enrichment and consumer class actions. Drug makers' US revenues would fall toward those international benchmarks, while consumers would pay less for the same medicines.
